data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism is internally inconsistent with the record's own distribution. It explains the asymmetry via mutation counts: compile.py has 'one mutation' against it, so 'a single shown-to-fail-first installation produces a clean 1-of-9 loss,' while ordinarily-guarded modules with 'four to seven mutations' lose nearly all. But compile.py lost 1 of 9 mutations — nine mutations, not one. If compile.py has MORE mutations than the 4/4 to 6/7 modules, the registry-size story is backwards: the module with the largest denominator (9) kept nearly all mutations, while modules with smaller denominators (4-7) lost nearly all. The mechanism predicts that a larger denominator should dilute a single selective event, yet the observed result is the exact opposite of what 'the denominator is small enough for a single selective event to dominate the fraction' would require — compile.py has the LARGER denominator and the SMALLER loss fraction. The claim that 'the one case with pre-installed failure is also the one case where the denominator is small enough for a single selective event to dominate' is directly contradicted by 1/9 versus 4/4-6/7: 9 is not smaller than 4-7.
